0.title: Ezra: The God Who Rebuilds
0.overview:
The book of Ezra opens in the middle of a sentence. If you were reading straight through the Hebrew Bible in its traditional order — Genesis, Exodus … Kings, Chronicles — you would turn the last page of 2 Chronicles and find Ezra beginning with its final two verses verbatim. "Thus says Cyrus king of Persia …" The exile is over. The story that seemed to have ended in ash and silence suddenly surges forward. The God Who Rebuilds has not finished speaking.

Ezra-Nehemiah was a single scroll in the Hebrew canon, later divided in the Septuagint tradition. The two books form a continuous narrative of the restoration community stretching from 538 BC (Cyrus's decree) to approximately 433 BC (Nehemiah's second governorship). Ezra covers two major movements separated by nearly sixty years of silence: the first return under Zerubbabel (chs. 1–6, 538–516 BC) and the second return under Ezra himself (chs. 7–10, 458 BC). The gap of fifty-eight years between chapter 6 and chapter 7 is not mentioned; the reader must supply it — a reminder that God's purposes are never rushed and never abandoned.

Historical Background. The Babylonian exile began in stages: Nebuchadnezzar took captives in 605 BC (including Daniel), again in 597 BC (including Ezekiel), and finally destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon's temple in 586 BC. The prophet Jeremiah had predicted the exile would last seventy years (Jer. 25:11–12; 29:10), and the Chronicler understood Cyrus's decree as the precise fulfillment of that prophecy (2 Chr. 36:21–22). In 539 BC, Cyrus the Great of Persia conquered Babylon without a battle — Herodotus and the Cyrus Cylinder alike attest that he entered the city as a liberator. His policy of repatriating conquered peoples and restoring their temples was both politically shrewd and, in Judah's case, providentially ordained. The LORD moved in Cyrus's heart before Cyrus moved his armies.

Structure. The book divides cleanly into two halves. Chapters 1–6 narrate the first return (the golah, the exilic community) under Zerubbabel the governor and Jeshua the high priest. They rebuild the altar, lay the foundation, face fierce opposition, fall silent for sixteen years, and then — stirred by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah — complete and dedicate the Second Temple in 516 BC. Chapters 7–10 introduce Ezra the scribe-priest, who arrives in Jerusalem in 458 BC under Artaxerxes I with a royal mandate to teach the law. His mission is immediately convulsed by the crisis of intermarriage with pagan neighbors. The book closes not with triumph but with a sobering covenant renewal and a long list of offenders — an ending that is both honest and hopeful.

Key Theological Themes. First, the sovereignty of God over pagan kings. Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes all serve the purposes of YHWH without knowing it. "The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will" (Prov. 21:1). Second, the remnant theology: God preserves a faithful core through catastrophe, and from that small, improbable seed he grows his purposes forward. Third, the priority of worship: the altar is rebuilt before the foundation is laid (3:2–3). Atonement precedes construction; the cross precedes the church. Fourth, the word of God as the engine of reform: Ezra's program begins with Torah-study (7:10) and culminates in public reading and exposition (Neh. 8). Scripture is not decoration; it is the load-bearing wall of the renewed community. Fifth, intercessory identification: Ezra's great prayer in chapter 9, confessing sins he did not personally commit, prefigures the solidarity of the true High Priest who takes the guilt of his people as his own.

Christological Connections. As Derek Kidner notes in his Tyndale commentary, the entire restoration narrative is a acted parable of the gospel: exile as judgment, the divine summons to "go up" as the call of grace, the rebuilt altar as the atonement that makes all other building possible. Cyrus is explicitly called God's "anointed" (mashiach, Isa. 45:1) — a striking type of the greater Deliverer who not only issues the upward summons but pays the price to make it possible. Ezra himself, as scribe-priest who perfectly integrates study, obedience, and teaching (7:10), is a type of Christ who came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5:17). And Ezra's weeping, self-identifying prayer over the community's sin anticipates the Gethsemane solidarity of the Son of God with sinners he had not harmed.

The Hand of the LORD. The governing phrase of chapters 7–10 is "the hand of the LORD his God was on him" (7:6, 9, 28; 8:18, 22, 31). This is not mere piety. It is the author's theological explanation for everything Ezra accomplished. The hand of the LORD — the executive power of the Creator himself — was the reason a single scribe could walk six hundred miles through hostile territory with no military escort, carrying the nation's hope in the law of God. May those who preach this book preach with that same hand upon them.

1.title: The Stirred Heart: Cyrus, the Decree, and the Upward Call
1.text: "In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom …" (Ezra 1:1)
1.overview:
The book begins where 2 Chronicles ends — with the same proclamation, almost the same words, the seam between the books deliberately visible, the story emphatically continuous. The exile is not God's last word. Cyrus's decree in 538 BC is. The opening verse does two things at once: it names the human agent (Cyrus) and the divine Author (the LORD), holding both together without apology. This is the Reformed doctrine of providence in narrative form: God governs history through secondary causes, but he governs it absolutely.

R.C. Sproul used to say that the most dangerous four words in the Christian vocabulary are "without God's permission." Nothing in Ezra 1 happens without his permission — or rather, without his initiative. He stirred the spirit of Cyrus (v. 1), he stirred the spirits of the returnees (v. 5), and he moved the neighbors of the returnees to give silver and gold (v. 6). The entire chapter is a cascade of divine action through human agency.

sections.title: The Word Fulfilled: Prophecy, Persia, and Providence (vv. 1–4)
sections.commentary:
The chapter opens with a stunning claim: the decree of a pagan king was the fulfillment of a Hebrew prophet's word spoken decades earlier. Jeremiah had said the exile would last seventy years (Jer. 25:11; 29:10); Isaiah had named Cyrus by name as the LORD's shepherd and anointed (Isa. 44:28; 45:1) — remarkable prophecies uttered more than a century before Cyrus was born. The convergence of these predictions in a single historical moment is the author's way of saying: the God of Israel is the Lord of world history.

The phrase "the LORD stirred up the spirit" (he'ir YHWH et-ruach) is crucial. The Hebrew verb 'ur means to rouse from sleep, to awaken. Cyrus was asleep to YHWH's purposes; God woke him up to them. The Cyrus Cylinder — the actual clay barrel inscription in which Cyrus describes his conquest of Babylon — uses strikingly similar language, claiming that the Babylonian god Marduk "scanned and looked through all the countries, searching for a righteous ruler." The author of Ezra does not dispute Cyrus's political self-understanding; he simply reassigns the credit. It was not Marduk who stirred Cyrus — it was YHWH. As Calvin comments on this verse: "Whenever kings do anything praiseworthy, we must remember that God holds their hearts in his hand."

The decree (vv. 2–4) is remarkable in its scope: Cyrus acknowledges that YHWH, the God of heaven, has given him all the kingdoms of the earth and has charged him to build a house in Jerusalem. Whether Cyrus was a genuine monotheist is debated; his cylinder shows he used similar language for Marduk. But the theological point stands: God can use a king who does not fully know him to accomplish purposes that serve his kingdom. H.G.M. Williamson notes that the decree has two parts — permission to go up to Jerusalem (v. 3) and a summons to the neighbors to provide resources (v. 4). The parallels with the Exodus are unmistakable: Israel leaving Egypt with silver and gold given by their neighbors (Exod. 12:35–36). A new Exodus is beginning. The Second Exodus typology will run through the entire book.

The word ya'al — "let him go up" (v. 3) — is the same upward summons that will govern the theology of return throughout Ezra. It is a pilgrim's word, an ascent-word, the word of someone moving toward Mount Zion. Alistair Begg has noted that this is not a passive permission but an active stirring: God does not merely allow the return; he creates the desire for it in human hearts. The same dynamic governs every conversion: the one who comes to Christ comes because the Father draws him (John 6:44), yet comes freely and willingly, because the drawing is a stirring of the spirit, not a coercion of the will.

sections.title: Stirred Spirits: The Response of the Community (v. 5)
sections.commentary:
Verse 5 is one of the most theologically loaded single verses in the book: "Then rose up the heads of the fathers' houses of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up to build the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem." Three things deserve careful attention.

First, the sovereignty of God in the stirring: "everyone whose spirit God had stirred." Not everyone went. Of the Jews in Babylon, only 42,360 returned in the first wave. The majority stayed — many had built houses, planted vineyards, achieved prosperity, exactly as Jeremiah had counseled them to do (Jer. 29:5–7). The returning minority were not superior in virtue; they were sovereign in divine calling. God stirred their spirits; he did not stir others'. This is remnant theology in action, and it prefigures the New Testament reality that not all who hear the gospel believe it — only those whose hearts are opened by the Spirit (Acts 16:14).

Second, the full participation of the tribal and religious leadership: heads of fathers' houses, priests, and Levites. The community of return was not a ragged mob of idealists; it was an ordered covenant community, organized according to the patterns of the Mosaic economy. Iain Duguid observes that the reconstituted community bears the marks of the old Israel, even in exile — the tribal structures, the priestly families, the Levitical orders. The continuity is deliberate: this is not a new thing God is doing; it is the old thing God is restoring.

Third, the purpose: "to go up to build the house of the LORD." The goal from the first moment is not self-preservation or national restoration in a political sense; it is temple-building, the reestablishment of the place where God dwells among his people. The book is, at its heart, about the dwelling of God with humanity — which is why the New Testament will describe the church as God's temple (1 Cor. 3:16) and the consummation as the new Jerusalem in which God himself is the temple (Rev. 21:22). Every brick of Zerubbabel's temple is a parable of that final reality.

sections.title: The New Exodus: Giving, Going, and the Gifts of Neighbors (vv. 6–11)
sections.commentary:
The parallels with the first Exodus intensify in these verses. Just as Israel left Egypt laden with the silver and gold of their Egyptian neighbors (Exod. 12:35–36), so the returning exiles are strengthened by their neighbors with "vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, with beasts, and with costly wares, besides all that was freely offered" (v. 6). The language of "freewill offering" (nedavah) will recur throughout the book — it is the vocabulary of Exodus-era generosity, of the tabernacle-building campaign in Exodus 35–36 when the people brought so much that Moses had to tell them to stop.

The vessels of the temple (vv. 7–11) deserve extended attention. Nebuchadnezzar had carried them to Babylon and placed them in the house of his gods (2 Kgs. 25:14–15; Dan. 1:2) — a liturgical act of conquest, the trophies of a defeated deity. Now Cyrus counts them out, has them catalogued (we are given the precise inventory: 30 gold basins, 1,000 silver basins, 29 censers, etc., totaling 5,400 items), and returns them. Derek Kidner writes: "The restoration of the vessels was a statement that the God of Israel was not defeated. His temple vessels had not been permanent spoils; they had been borrowed by history for a season." The careful accounting — "Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah" receives them — is the author's way of insisting on the legal, legitimate continuity of the restoration community with the pre-exilic community. These are the same vessels; this is the same people; this is the same God.

Sheshbazzar is a puzzling figure who disappears after chapter 1. He may be identical with Zerubbabel (his Babylonian name vs. his Hebrew name), or he may be a distinct figure who handed off leadership to Zerubbabel. Williamson leans toward identification; Kidner preserves the distinction. Either way, his role here is transitional and administrative: he is the official custodian of the vessels, the carrier of the nation's liturgical memory from Babylon to Jerusalem. The preacher might pause here to note that one of the great privileges of ministry is to be a carrier of the sacred vessels — the word of God, the sacraments, the apostolic tradition — from generation to generation.

1.theology:
Providence and the Stirred Heart. Ezra 1 is perhaps the clearest Old Testament text for what Reformed theology calls "concurrence" — the doctrine that God's sovereign action and human free action operate simultaneously at different levels without canceling each other. Cyrus freely issued his decree; the returnees freely chose to go up; the neighbors freely gave. And behind every one of these free choices was the prior action of God who stirred, moved, and ordained. R.C. Sproul: "There is not one maverick molecule in the universe." Ezra 1 is the narrative proof of that claim.

The Second Exodus. The Exodus typology is not incidental decoration; it is the organizing theological framework of the entire book. The return from Babylon is presented as a new Exodus: the nations give silver and gold, a leader arises to take the community through a long journey to the promised land, and they arrive to rebuild the place of God's presence. This typology will reach its climax in Christ, who accomplishes the ultimate Exodus (Luke 9:31, where "departure" is literally exodos) — leading his people out of the Egypt of sin through the Red Sea of death into the promised land of resurrection life.
1.examples:
Then: The Jews in Babylon had every reason to stay. They were comfortable, established, prosperous. God's call to return was a call to leave security for a ruined city, a difficult journey, and an uncertain future. The 42,360 who went were the ones whose spirits God had stirred — they felt the pull of Jerusalem more keenly than the comfort of Babylon. They were not heroes; they were summoned people.

Now: Every Christian is a person whose spirit God has stirred. You did not choose Christ because you were spiritually acute; you came because the Father drew you (John 6:44), because the Spirit awakened you from the sleep of spiritual death (Eph. 2:1–5). This should produce profound humility — "What do you have that you did not receive?" (1 Cor. 4:7) — and profound gratitude. The same stirring that brought the exiles home brings sinners to Christ. And the same God who gave the exiles a clear commission — "go up, build the house of the LORD" — gives every believer a clear vocation: seek first the kingdom of God.

2.title: The Names God Keeps: The List of the Returning Remnant
2.text: "These were the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of those exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried captive to Babylonia. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town." (Ezra 2:1)
2.overview:
Modern readers skim lists. Ancient readers read them with tears. The genealogical register of Ezra 2 — 42,360 people, their servants, their animals, their geographic destinations — is not a boring interruption of the narrative; it is the narrative's theological core. These are the names God kept through seventy years of exile. Derek Kidner: "The roll-call of the remnant is nothing less than the register of the faithful, the evidence that God's purposes do not miscarry."

The list is carefully structured: lay families by ancestors (vv. 3–20), lay families by towns (vv. 21–35), priests (vv. 36–39), Levites (vv. 40–42), temple servants (vv. 43–58), those of uncertain ancestry (vv. 59–63), and finally the grand total with animals (vv. 64–67). The precision is intentional. God is a God of particulars. He does not save "humanity" in the abstract; he saves named individuals whom he calls by name.

sections.title: The Leaders and the Lay Families (vv. 1–35)
sections.commentary:
The list opens with twelve named leaders (v. 2) — Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah — a detail that is theologically significant. Twelve leaders for twelve tribes: the restoration community is deliberately presented as a reconstituted Israel, the full covenant people, even though historically it was predominantly Judah and Benjamin. The number twelve reaches back to the patriarchs and forward to the twelve apostles whom Jesus appointed as the foundation of the new Israel (Rev. 21:14). The symbolic arithmetic of God's covenant community runs through Scripture like a golden thread.

Zerubbabel heads the list. He is the grandson of King Jehoiachin (1 Chr. 3:17–19), the last legitimate Davidic king before the exile. His presence at the head of the returning community is a statement about the Davidic covenant: the exile did not end the royal line. The seed of David survived Babylon. The prophets Haggai and Zechariah would later associate messianic expectations with Zerubbabel specifically (Hag. 2:23; Zech. 4:6–10), though he himself was never king. He is a type of the greater Son of David who will return not from Babylon but from the far country of death itself.

The lay families are listed first by ancestral name (vv. 3–20) and then by town of origin (vv. 21–35). Both systems of identification appear simultaneously, reminding us that these people are connected both to a family history (who they are) and a geographic home (where they belong). The theology of belonging — to a people, to a place, to a story — is not incidental to Israel's identity. It is constitutive. Alistair Begg has observed that one of the marks of genuine spiritual renewal is exactly this recovery of identity: we know who we are (children of the covenant), where we are going (the city of God), and why (to worship).

The numbers in the list present a minor textual challenge: the individual totals (approximately 29,818 by count) do not add up to 42,360 (v. 64). The parallel list in Nehemiah 7 has different numbers. Williamson suggests the 42,360 includes women and children not enumerated in the named heads-of-household lists, while the Nehemiah discrepancies reflect different manuscript traditions of the same underlying document. The discrepancy has been used by critical scholars to undermine the historicity of the text; but as Kidner wisely notes, "the minutiae of ancient record-keeping are not always recoverable, and the theological point — that God kept precise account of his people — is not undermined by scribal variation in transmission."

sections.title: Priests, Levites, and Temple Servants (vv. 36–58)
sections.commentary:
The priestly families (vv. 36–39) number 4,289 — a significant proportion of the total returnees, indicating how central the priestly community was to the restoration project. Four priestly families are named: Jedaiah, Immer, Pashhur, and Harim. These are the families that will bear the weight of the renewed sacrificial system. Their presence in the list is not just demographic; it is a statement that the covenant-mediation structure of Israel — the elaborate Mosaic economy of priests, offerings, and atonement — is being reconstituted in the land.

The Levites (vv. 40–42) are conspicuously fewer: only 341, a number that will cause concern in Ezra 8:15 when Ezra finds no Levites among his party and has to send for them. The Nethinim (temple servants, vv. 43–54) and the sons of Solomon's servants (vv. 55–57) total 392. These groups — the Nethinim particularly — are of uncertain origin; some scholars connect them with the Gibeonites of Joshua 9 who became "hewers of wood and drawers of water" for the sanctuary. Their inclusion in the list is noteworthy: even those of ambiguous ethnic ancestry who had attached themselves to the covenant community are counted among the returnees.

The section on those of uncertain genealogy (vv. 59–63) is pastorally important. Certain priestly families could not prove their lineage and were therefore excluded from priestly service "until a priest with Urim and Thummim" should arise to adjudicate the matter (v. 63). This is an honest acknowledgment of a real pastoral dilemma: the community needed to maintain the integrity of priestly service (which required legitimate Aaronic descent) while also being merciful to those whose records had been lost in the catastrophe of exile. The Urim and Thummim — the oracular devices by which God communicated to Israel through the high priest — had apparently not functioned in the post-exilic period. The community was waiting for a definitive divine word on contested matters. The preacher may note the eschatological resonance: we too are waiting for the final clarification of what has been obscured, the full disclosure of the sons of God (Rom. 8:19).

sections.title: The Grand Total and the Freewill Offerings (vv. 64–70)
sections.commentary:
The grand total of 42,360 (v. 64) with 7,337 servants and 200 singing men and women (v. 65) is followed immediately by the freewill offerings for the work of the house of God (vv. 68–69). The juxtaposition is deliberate: the community is numbered, and then the community gives. The offering totals are staggering by ancient standards: 61,000 darics of gold, 5,000 minas of silver, and 100 priestly garments. A daric was the standard Persian gold coin; 61,000 darics represents an enormous sum, demonstrating that at least some of the returnees had prospered in Babylon and were willing to bring their wealth back to the service of God.

The freewill offering (nedavah) recalls the great Exodus giving for the tabernacle (Exod. 35:4–29) and David's offering for the temple (1 Chr. 29:1–9). In all three instances, the giving is voluntary, generous, and connected to a building project that serves the presence of God. Calvin comments: "Whenever God stirs men to contribute to the building of his house, it is a mark of singular grace — for it is he who both supplies the material and creates the desire to give it." The offerings are the evidence that the stirred spirit of chapter 1 has produced tangible, costly action. Genuine spiritual renewal always expresses itself in open-handed generosity.

The chapter closes with the returnees settled in their towns (v. 70). It is a quiet ending to a loud list — the 42,360 dispersing to their ancestral villages, planting gardens, opening doors, beginning the long work of rebuilding. The great reversal has begun. The God who scattered has now gathered; the God who brought exile has now brought home. And over every one of those 42,360 names — each person who has come up from the confusion of Babylon to the specificity of a home and a town — the same God watches who watched over them in exile. He keeps the names he keeps.

2.theology:
The Theology of the List. Eugene Peterson observed that one of the neglected disciplines of biblical preaching is the willingness to linger in the lists. Ezra 2 rewards that lingering. The list is a theological argument: God's covenant faithfulness is not abstract but particular. He did not preserve "the Jewish people" as an idea; he preserved Jedaiah's family, the men of Bethlehem, the sons of Harim. The New Testament equivalent is the roll of names in Romans 16 — Phoebe, Aquila, Priscilla, Andronicus — the real, named people who make up the body of Christ. The God of the Bible is a God who knows our names.

Remnant and Election. The 42,360 are not the whole of Israel. They are the remnant — the she'erit, the surviving portion. Paul will draw on this concept in Romans 9–11 to explain why not all ethnic Israel is saved: "So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace" (Rom. 11:5). The Ezra community is the Old Testament precedent for that New Testament teaching. Grace does not save categories; it summons persons. And it never fails to preserve the seed it has chosen.
2.examples:
Then: For the original readers of Ezra — perhaps gathered in Nehemiah's Jerusalem, listening to the law being read — the list of chapter 2 would have functioned like a family Bible, or the names on a war memorial. These were our people, the ones who risked the journey. To hear your grandfather's name in the list was to understand yourself as part of a story that preceded you and would outlast you.

Now: The Book of Life (Rev. 20:15; 21:27) is the ultimate register of the remnant. Every person whose name is written there has been "stirred" by the Spirit of God, drawn by the Father, born from above. The Christian's confidence in the face of judgment is not that they were worthy to be listed, but that the God who kept 42,360 names through seventy years of Babylonian exile is the God who keeps his people to the end. "I know my own and my own know me" (John 10:14) — the Good Shepherd's census is perfect and complete.

3.title: The Altar Before the Temple: Worship, Weeping, and the Shout of Joy
3.text: "When the seventh month came, and the children of Israel were in the towns, the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem. Then arose Jeshua the son of Jozadak, with his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel with his kinsmen, and they built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings on it …" (Ezra 3:1–2)
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the theological heart of Ezra 1–6. Two great events occur here: the rebuilding of the altar (vv. 1–7) and the laying of the temple foundation with its double response of weeping and shouting (vv. 8–13). Both events carry enormous theological freight. The altar before the temple establishes the liturgical order: atonement precedes construction, worship precedes work, the cross precedes the church. And the mixed response to the foundation — old men weeping, young men shouting, the sounds indistinguishable — is one of the most psychologically and spiritually true moments in all of Scripture.

Sinclair Ferguson has described this chapter as "the pattern of all genuine renewal": the community gathers, worship is reestablished, the foundation is laid, and the response is complex — because genuine encounters with God always are. Triumphalism and grief coexist in the people of God. We live between the "already" and the "not yet," between the foundation and the completion, between what God has begun and what he has promised.

sections.title: The Altar First: Atonement Before Construction (vv. 1–7)
sections.commentary:
The returnees have been in the land since approximately 537 BC. But the first corporate act — recorded in the seventh month, which is the month of the great festivals (Lev. 23) — is not to clear rubble or survey building sites. It is to rebuild the altar. Jeshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor lead the community in this act, and the theological priority is unmistakable: before there is a house for God, there must be an altar. Before the building goes up, the sacrifice must be offered. The logic is Mosaic: at Sinai, the tabernacle was the dwelling place, but the altar of burnt offering stood at its entrance — the first thing encountered by anyone approaching God.

Verse 3 is particularly striking: "They set the altar in its place, for fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands, and they offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD, burnt offerings morning and evening." The altar was built in fear. The surrounding peoples were hostile (the opposition of chapter 4 had not yet begun formally, but the threat was palpable). The correct response to fear — then and now — is not to delay worship until the threat is past, but to worship precisely because the threat is real. The altar is not the place of spiritual luxury; it is the place of spiritual necessity. When you are afraid, you go to the altar. When the enemies surround you, you offer the morning and evening sacrifice.

John MacArthur has preached Ezra 3:3 as the pattern of courage in ministry: "The altar was set up in spite of the fear, not in the absence of it." The community did not wait for security; they established the means of grace under threat and trusted that the God to whom they were offering would protect his own worship. The Feast of Booths (Tabernacles, v. 4) — the great harvest festival of Leviticus 23:33–43 — was observed fully, with freewill offerings on top of the prescribed number. When people are genuinely restored to God, their giving exceeds the minimum. The spirit of the law finds expression in generosity beyond the letter.

The procurement of cedar from Lebanon (v. 7) via Sidon and Tyre, with payment authorized by Cyrus's decree, is a deliberate echo of Solomon's temple-building (1 Kgs. 5:1–11). The author is drawing the continuity line clearly: this is not a new thing; it is the restoration of the old thing. The God who built through Solomon will build through Zerubbabel. The means are the same; the God is the same; the purpose is the same. The temple that is being rebuilt is not a lesser substitute but the legitimate continuation of the one that was destroyed.

sections.title: The Foundation Laid: The Second Year and the Levitical Song (vv. 8–11)
sections.commentary:
In the second year of their return — 536 BC — Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and all who had come from the captivity begin the formal work of building the house of the LORD. The organizational detail of verse 8 is noteworthy: Levites twenty years old and upward are appointed to oversee the work (cf. Num. 8:24, where the age of Levitical service began at twenty-five; this lower threshold reflects both the urgency of the project and the adaptation of Mosaic legislation to a new context). The sons of Jeshua and of Kadmiel are named as the supervisors — named individuals, accountable for specific work. God's building projects are not vague spiritual aspirations; they are organized, supervised, and accountable.

The foundational moment arrives in verses 10–11, and the author's literary artistry is at its finest. When the builders lay the foundation of the temple, the priests stand in their vestments with trumpets, and the Levites with cymbals, "to praise the LORD, according to the directions of David king of Israel." The reference to Davidic liturgical order is another continuity marker: the temple worship being reestablished follows the pattern David established (1 Chr. 15–16, 23–25). Even in rebuilding, the community is not improvising; it is recovering a received tradition.

The song they sing (v. 11) is a fragment of what appears to be Psalm 136 or a similar responsorial psalm: "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel." The Hebrew word is chesed — steadfast love, covenant faithfulness, lovingkindness. This is the word that defines YHWH's character in his self-revelation to Moses (Exod. 34:6–7) and echoes through the Psalter like a refrain. To sing chesed over a ruined foundation is an act of extraordinary faith: we are affirming that God's covenant love survived the exile, survived Babylon, survived the death of the nation, and is now — right here, on this rubble-strewn hilltop — being manifested again in stones and mortar and Levitical song.

sections.title: The Weeping and the Shouting: The Indistinguishable Sounds (vv. 12–13)
sections.commentary:
These two verses are among the most moving in the entire Old Testament. The author carefully describes two simultaneous responses to the laying of the foundation: the old priests and Levites and family heads who had seen Solomon's temple wept aloud, while many others shouted for joy — "so that the people could not distinguish the sound of the joyful shout from the sound of the people's weeping, for the people shouted with a great shout, and the sound was heard far away."

The weeping of the old men is the grief of holy memory and holy comparison. They had seen the first temple — the incomparable structure Solomon built over seven years with 180,000 workers, lined with gold, housing the ark of the covenant and the Shekinah glory. They remembered the fire coming down from heaven (2 Chr. 7:1). Now they see a modest foundation on a ruined hilltop, with far fewer workers and far fewer resources, and they weep. Their tears are not faithless; they are honest. Kidner: "Their tears were not a failure of faith but a token of it — they remembered what God had done before, and the comparison wounded them." It is possible to be both genuinely grateful for what God is doing and genuinely grieved by the gap between what is and what was, or what should be.

The shouting of the young is the joy of those who have never seen the temple, who know only exile and its ending. For them, any foundation is a miracle. They have no memory of Solomonic grandeur against which to measure this modest beginning; they have only the promise that God would restore his people, and here — here! — is the evidence that the promise is being kept. Their joy is not shallow; it is theologically appropriate. Every stone of this foundation is a trophy of grace.

And the sounds cannot be told apart. This is the author's most profound theological observation: the grief of holy memory and the joy of present grace are simultaneously present in the community of God, and they are not in tension — they are harmonized into a single, unanalyzable cry that is heard far away. Alistair Begg has preached this passage as the pattern of the Christian life lived between the Testaments: we know what God has done (in Christ, in history, in our own lives), we grieve the gap between that and the present reality, and we shout for joy that the foundation has been laid. The two sounds are not contradictory; they are the stereo of the gospel — the minor key of not yet harmonized with the major key of already.

The Christological connection is inescapable. At Calvary, the sound of lamentation (Mary weeping, the disciples scattered) and the sound of cosmic triumph (it is finished, the veil torn) were simultaneous and indistinguishable to human ears in that moment. Only in retrospect — in resurrection — did the two sounds sort themselves out. The community at Ezra 3 lives in that Calvary-shaped moment: foundation laid, building incomplete, weeping and shouting at once.

3.theology:
The Altar Before the Temple. The theological order of Ezra 3 — altar rebuilt (vv. 1–7) before foundation laid (vv. 8–13) — is the order of the gospel. You cannot build the house of God on an unatoned foundation. The altar represents the propitiation that makes all approach to God possible; the temple represents the dwelling that propitiation enables. In the New Testament, Christ is both the altar (the place of atonement, Heb. 13:10) and the temple (the dwelling of God, John 2:19–21). The cross precedes the church; atonement precedes community. Any ecclesiology that bypasses the altar is built on sand.

Grief and Joy in Tension. The weeping and shouting of Ezra 3:12–13 establishes what might be called the "eschatological key" in which the community of God always lives: the tension between the already and the not yet, between what God has begun and what he has promised, between the foundation and the consummation. Paul captures the same tension in Romans 8: groaning with the creation (grief) while being confident in the hope of glory (joy). The two sounds do not cancel each other; they enrich each other. A community that knows only shouting has forgotten the depth of what was lost; a community that knows only weeping has forgotten the certainty of what has been promised.
3.examples:
Then: The old men's tears were a form of prophecy — they knew, better than anyone, how far short this foundation fell of what the temple should be. And they were right. The Second Temple, for all its later magnificence under Herod, never housed the ark, never saw the Shekinah glory return, never heard the Urim and Thummim speak. Yet it was in this temple that the Son of God himself would one day stand and say, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The old men's tears were answered beyond their imagining.

Now: Every church that gathers for worship lives in this tension. We remember what the church has been at its best — Pentecost, the Reformation, revival — and we see the gap between that and our present reality. We grieve. And simultaneously, we shout: the foundation is Jesus Christ, the altar has been built at Calvary, the Spirit has been poured out, the church exists. The two sounds together constitute authentic Christian worship — not triumphalism, not despair, but the honest, faith-filled cry of a people who know both what has been lost and what has been given.

4.title: The Long Delay: Opposition, Discouragement, and Silence
4.text: "Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel, they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of fathers' houses and said to them, 'Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do …' But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of fathers' houses in Israel said to them, 'You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God …'" (Ezra 4:1–3)
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is one of the most structurally complex — and theologically instructive — chapters in the Old Testament. On the surface it narrates the opposition that brought the temple-building project to a halt from approximately 536 BC to 520 BC — a silence of sixteen years. But the author has deliberately arranged his material non-chronologically: verses 6–23 describe letters written to Artaxerxes (who reigned 465–424 BC, long after the temple was completed) about the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. The author is not confused; he is making a theological point. Opposition is not a single incident; it is a pattern. The enemies of God's building project do not give up.

The chapter teaches three things that every minister and church planter needs to hear: first, opposition often arrives disguised as cooperation (vv. 1–5); second, persistent opposition can silence the people of God for years (v. 24); and third, the silence is not the final word. The God who began the building will resume it.

sections.title: The Offer of Help: Opposition in Disguise (vv. 1–5)
sections.commentary:
The opening gambit of the adversaries is superficially generous: "Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him ever since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria who brought us here" (v. 2). The people speaking are the mixed population that Assyria had imported into the Northern Kingdom after deporting Israel in 722 BC — the ancestors of the later Samaritans. They do worship YHWH, but alongside other gods (cf. 2 Kgs. 17:24–41). Their claim to be co-worshippers is half true, which makes it the more dangerous. A half-true offer of help is more threatening to the integrity of the community than an outright attack.

Zerubbabel's refusal (v. 3) is sometimes criticized as exclusionary, even xenophobic. The charge misses the theological point entirely. Williamson: "The issue is not ethnicity but covenant identity. The returning exiles understood themselves as the legitimate continuation of the covenant community, charged with rebuilding the specific sanctuary that YHWH had designated. To allow outside parties — even sincere ones — to share in the building of YHWH's house was to compromise the community's identity as the covenant people." The decree of Cyrus had been issued to specific beneficiaries; the building project was a covenant community project. This is not racial exclusion; it is covenant precision.

The preacher may draw a pointed application: not every offer of help in kingdom work is from a kingdom spirit. Ecumenical generosity that blurs the boundaries of the gospel — accepting "co-builders" who worship a Jesus alongside other saviors — is not hospitality; it is syncretism. Zerubbabel's discernment in this moment is a pattern for pastoral leadership in every age. The courage to say "you have nothing to do with us" is sometimes the most important thing a leader can say. Refusing the wrong help is as crucial as accepting the right.

The consequence is immediate: "Then the people of the land discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build and hired counselors against them to frustrate their purpose" (vv. 4–5). The word "discouraged" is merafim yedey in Hebrew — literally "weakening their hands." Opposition aims at the hands, the working capacity of the community. When your hands are weakened by fear, the work stops. The sixteen-year silence (v. 24) is not laziness; it is the result of sustained, organized, and financially resourced opposition. The enemies hired lobbyists.

sections.title: Letters to Persia: The Pattern of Persistent Opposition (vv. 6–23)
sections.commentary:
The author now inserts, parenthetically, examples of the same kind of opposition at later dates — letters written to Ahasuerus (Xerxes, vv. 6) and Artaxerxes (vv. 7–23) about Jerusalem's rebuilding. This is not a chronological error; it is a rhetorical technique. The author is showing that the pattern of opposition in Zerubbabel's day was not unique; it persisted under every Persian king. The enemies of the restoration are persistent, clever, and well-connected.

The letter to Artaxerxes (vv. 11–16) is a masterpiece of political manipulation. It appeals to the king's self-interest ("this city is a rebellious city," v. 12), invokes historical precedent ("search in the book of the records," v. 15), and warns of financial loss ("if this city is rebuilt … you will have no possession in the province Beyond the River," v. 16). None of these charges are precisely false; Jerusalem had a history of rebellion. But they are marshaled selectively and maliciously to serve the opponents' agenda. Kidner: "This is the technique of the half-truth deployed against the whole truth — more dangerous than an outright lie because it cannot simply be dismissed."

Artaxerxes' response (vv. 17–22) is to order a halt to the building — an order that is enforced by force (v. 23). This is a genuine crisis. The king of Persia — whose predecessor Cyrus had commissioned the building, and whose authorization the community depended on — has now countermanded the commission. The legal ground has shifted. The community is in a worse position than before: not just resisted by local opponents but under royal prohibition. The preacher should pause here to honor the reality of this: some setbacks in ministry are not mere obstacles; they are comprehensive reversals that seem to undo everything that has been built. The question is not whether such setbacks occur but what the community does when they do.

The answer, in Ezra's narrative, is that God sends prophets (5:1). But that answer comes only after sixteen years of silence. The silence is real; the delay is real; the discouragement is real. God does not minimize it. He enters it.

sections.title: The Work Ceases: Sixteen Years of Silence (v. 24)
sections.commentary:
Verse 24 is the hinge of the chapter and, in a sense, of the entire first half of the book: "Then the work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem stopped, and it ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia." From 536 BC to 520 BC — sixteen years. The foundation had been laid with weeping and shouting; and now there is neither. The building has stopped. The rubble remains. The altar is functioning, but the house of God is unbuilt.

This is one of the most sobering verses in the Old Testament for those involved in long-term ministry. Sixteen years is not a setback; it is a generation. Children born when the foundation was laid are teenagers when the building resumes. The community that began with stirred spirits and freewill offerings has become a community accustomed to compromise — people who have started building their own houses (cf. Hag. 1:4) while the LORD's house lies in ruins.

John Stott once said that the greatest danger in ministry is not persecution but comfort. The people of Ezra 4 were not in Babylon; they were in the land. They had their altar and their sacrifices. They had built houses and planted vineyards. The urgency of Zerubbabel's day — the stirred spirit, the sense of divine commission — had been gradually absorbed by the demands of ordinary life. It took the prophetic shock of Haggai and Zechariah to break through. The preacher should ask: what are the contemporary equivalents of the stopped work? What foundations in our own communities have been laid but not built upon, because opposition, comfort, and the passage of time have weakened our hands?

4.theology:
Opposition as Spiritual Reality. Ezra 4 establishes that opposition to God's building project is not an accident or an anomaly; it is a structural feature of kingdom work in a fallen world. The enemies use every available tool: political manipulation, legal prohibition, financial pressure, and — most insidiously — the offer of help that would compromise the community's identity. Paul's observation that "we do not wrestle against flesh and blood" (Eph. 6:12) is the New Testament framework for reading this chapter: behind the human opponents are spiritual forces hostile to the kingdom of God.

The Silence of God and the Silence of the Community. Sixteen years of silence is not sixteen years of divine abandonment. Haggai 1:13 will later record: "I am with you, declares the LORD." God's presence was not conditional on the community's productivity. But the community's experience of God's blessing was conditional on their obedience (Hag. 1:5–11): while they built their own houses, the dew was withheld from heaven and the soil from its produce. The sixteen-year silence is not punishment in the judicial sense; it is the natural consequence of a community that has stopped seeking first the kingdom of God.
4.examples:
Then: The Samaritan opponents were not cartoon villains. They had real political connections, real legal arguments, and real grievances born of decades of complex regional politics. The community in Jerusalem had to discern between legitimate concerns and bad-faith opposition — a discernment that required wisdom, courage, and a clear sense of their own identity and commission.

Now: Every church, every Christian ministry, every individual disciple will encounter the kind of opposition described in Ezra 4. It will come in the form of discouragement, legal obstruction, financial pressure, and — most commonly — the slow erosion of urgency by comfort and prosperity. The prescription is not stoicism but prophetic renewal: we need voices like Haggai and Zechariah to call us back to the work. And we need leaders like Zerubbabel who, when the prophets speak, get up and build (5:2).

5.title: The Prophets Arise: Haggai, Zechariah, and the Resumption of Work
5.text: "Now the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel who was over them. Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak arose and began to rebuild the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, supporting them." (Ezra 5:1–2)
5.overview:
After sixteen years of silence and stopped work, chapter 5 opens with an earthquake: the prophets arise. Haggai and Zechariah begin to preach, and the effect is immediate — the community gets up and builds. The author presents this causally: the prophetic word produces the building activity. This is one of the most vivid demonstrations in the Old Testament of the power of the proclaimed word to stir dormant obedience. The word of God spoken through human lips moves a stalled community from paralysis to action.

The chapter then narrates the resumption of opposition — new officials write to the new king Darius to inquire about the building's authorization. But this time the response will be different, because the documentary record is found and the decree of Cyrus is upheld. The community continues building during the inquiry (v. 5: "the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not stop them"), trusting that what God had authorized no human inquiry could ultimately revoke.

sections.title: The Prophetic Word Breaks the Silence (vv. 1–2)
sections.commentary:
These two verses are among the most encouraging in the Bible for those who preach and those who hear preaching. The situation before verse 1 is: sixteen years of stopped work, a community settled into comfortable spiritual mediocrity, the house of God unbuilt. After verse 2: the community is building. The connecting event is the prophetic word. Haggai and Zechariah "prophesied to the Jews … in the name of the God of Israel who was over them." They preached in God's name, with God's authority, about God's purposes. And it worked.

The books of Haggai and Zechariah provide the content of this preaching and are essential companions to Ezra 5–6. Haggai's first oracle (Hag. 1:2–11) is a sharp rebuke: "Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?" He connects the community's economic frustrations — poor harvests, inflation, drought — to their spiritual negligence. MacArthur: "Haggai is the prophet of priorities. His message is brutally simple: you are not prospering because you have your priorities inverted. Seek first the kingdom of God." Zechariah's opening oracle (Zech. 1:2–6) calls the community back to covenant faithfulness: "Return to me … and I will return to you."

The response in verse 2 is the pattern of all genuine reformation: "Then Zerubbabel … and Jeshua … arose and began to rebuild." The prophets spoke; the leaders arose; the people built. Word precedes action; proclamation precedes construction. This is why the Reformers insisted on preaching as the primary mark of the true church: notae ecclesiae — the true church is where the word of God is truly preached and the sacraments rightly administered. Where genuine biblical preaching occurs, the people of God get up and build. Where it ceases, they settle into their paneled houses.

"The prophets of God were with them, supporting them" (v. 2b). The preacher's role in the building project is not administrative but structural: the prophets provide the spiritual architecture within which the physical building can proceed. Iain Duguid: "The prophets did not do the building — Zerubbabel and Jeshua led that work. But the building could not have happened without the prophets. Word ministry and leadership ministry are mutually dependent in the work of God."

sections.title: Tattenai's Inquiry: Challenged but Not Stopped (vv. 3–17)
sections.commentary:
Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai arrive in Jerusalem to investigate the building project (v. 3). Their question is pointed: "Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this timber work?" (v. 4). It is the kind of challenge that could silence a community uncertain of its legal standing. But the author inserts a parenthetical of extraordinary theological weight: "But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not stop them until the report should reach Darius" (v. 5).

The eye of God. This is the counterpart to the "hand of God" theme that dominates chapters 7–8. The eye suggests watchfulness, oversight, protection. God is not unaware of the opposition; he sees it and sees through it. The community builds under official scrutiny because God's eye is on them — they are not reckless but protected. This is the pastoral message of the verse: the eye of God on his people does not exempt them from opposition but sustains them through it. As Sproul put it: "God does not remove the trials; he superintends them."

The elders' reply to Tattenai (vv. 11–16) is a model of courageous, historically grounded testimony. They identify themselves: "We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth" (v. 11) — not the servants of Zerubbabel, not the subjects of Persia, but the servants of the living God who made heaven and earth. They acknowledge the exile honestly: the God of heaven gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar because they provoked him. They do not suppress the painful history; they narrate it truthfully as the prelude to the current story of restoration. Then they cite Cyrus's decree and Sheshbazzar's role in laying the original foundation.

The letter to Darius (vv. 6–17) is a straightforward bureaucratic inquiry, but it carries enormous theological freight: the Persian imperial system, which destroyed the first temple through Nebuchadnezzar, is now being used to protect the building of the second. The mechanisms of empire — archival records, official letters, royal authority — are being conscripted into the service of God's purposes without the empire being aware of it. Providence works through bureaucracy. Williamson: "The author of Ezra delights in showing how the administrative machinery of the world's greatest empire became an instrument for the fulfillment of prophetic promises."

5.theology:
The Priority of the Prophetic Word. Ezra 5 establishes an axiom: the work of God in the community of God follows the word of God through the servants of God. Haggai and Zechariah did not build; they preached. But their preaching broke sixteen years of silence and paralysis. This is the New Testament pattern as well: "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ" (Rom. 10:17). The building of the church — its reformation, its revival, its growth — always follows the recovery of faithful biblical proclamation. The church declines when it silences the prophets; it advances when it hears them.

"The Eye of Their God." Verse 5 stands as one of the great comfort verses of the Old Testament for communities under pressure. God's watchfulness is not passive; in the Old Testament framework, the eye of God is the eye of the shepherd who counts his sheep (Ps. 121:3–4), the eye of the judge who sees what is done in secret (Prov. 15:3), and the eye of the Father who is not inattentive to sparrows (Matt. 10:29). The community builds, challenged and exposed, because the eye of God is upon them.
5.examples:
Then: Zerubbabel had been building a foundation since 536 BC, a project that had been stopped and then revived by prophetic preaching. When the governor arrives with an official inquiry, the community does not panic, produce documentation, or cease work. They continue building and give an honest, historically grounded answer. Their confidence is not in their legal position but in their theological certainty: the eye of their God is on them.

Now: When ministry faces official opposition — regulatory, cultural, institutional — the model of Ezra 5 is neither defiance nor compliance but truthful, courageous testimony combined with continued faithful work. The early church (Acts 4–5) follows exactly this pattern: challenged by the Sanhedrin, they give honest testimony about what they have seen and heard, and they continue preaching. They do not wait for the challenge to be resolved before they build. They build while the inquiry is ongoing, trusting that the eye of God is upon them.

6.title: The Temple Completed: Darius's Decree, Dedication, and Passover
6.text: "And the elders of the Jews built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. They finished their building by decree of the God of Israel and by decree of Cyrus and Darius and Artaxerxes king of Persia; and this house was finished on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king." (Ezra 6:14–15)
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is the great resolution of the first half of Ezra. The archive is searched, the decree of Cyrus is found, Darius issues a new decree in support of the building, the opposition is silenced, and — in a date that carries the weight of seventy years of prophetic promise — the temple is completed on the third day of Adar in the sixth year of Darius: 516 BC, exactly seventy years after Nebuchadnezzar burned Solomon's temple in 586 BC. Jeremiah's prophecy has been fulfilled to the year. The God who promised is the God who keeps.

The chapter closes with the first Passover celebrated in the rebuilt temple — a liturgical act that announces the completion of the second Exodus. The community that returned from Babylon, like Israel released from Egypt, now gathers to remember their deliverance at the table of the LORD. The first half of Ezra ends not with political triumph but with Passover lamb.

sections.title: The Archive Found: Darius's Decree (vv. 1–12)
sections.commentary:
King Darius orders a search of the royal archives (v. 1), and the original decree of Cyrus is found — not in Babylon, as expected, but in Ecbatana, the summer capital of the Medes and Persians (v. 2). The decree is specific about the dimensions of the temple (60 cubits high, 60 cubits wide, v. 3) and the source of funding (the royal treasury, v. 4). This is a remarkable administrative discovery: a decades-old decree of a previous emperor, filed in a summer palace, retrieved by bureaucratic diligence, and used to authorize and fund the building project of a minority population in a remote province.

God moves through filing systems. The Reformers loved to note that God uses the most mundane means to accomplish his purposes: a filing clerk who did his job, an archive that was maintained properly, a summer capital that happened to store the right document. Providence does not suspend the ordinary; it works through it. Kidner: "The recovery of the Cyrus scroll is one of those small, bureaucratic miracles that reveal how thoroughly God superintends the details of history."

Darius's response to the discovery is extravagant by any imperial standard (vv. 6–12): not only does he order the opposition to stand aside, but he commands that the costs of the building be paid from provincial taxes (v. 8), that daily supplies of animals for burnt offerings be provided (v. 9), and that whoever interferes with the decree be impaled on a timber pulled from his own house (v. 11). The penalty is deliberately comical in its severity — Darius is deploying imperial thunder on behalf of a small provincial temple. The irony is theologically rich: the king who controls armies and treasuries is now the administrative arm of the God of Israel's building project. "He who sits in the heavens laughs" (Ps. 2:4) — but he also uses the laughable instruments of earthly power to accomplish his purposes.

Verse 10 provides the explicit theological rationale for Darius's generosity: "that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons." The pagan king wants the prayers of the covenant community. This is a remarkable reversal: the community that was deported and humiliated is now in a position where the greatest power on earth solicits its intercessions. Paul's instruction to pray for kings and those in authority (1 Tim. 2:1–2) has deep roots in this pattern.

sections.title: The Temple Completed: Seventy Years Fulfilled (vv. 13–15)
sections.commentary:
Verses 14–15 are the climax of the first half of Ezra, and they deserve to be preached slowly. "And the elders of the Jews built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. They finished their building by decree of the God of Israel and by decree of Cyrus and Darius and Artaxerxes king of Persia; and this house was finished on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king."

Three things are worth unpacking. First, the triple decree: Cyrus's original authorization, Darius's reaffirmation, and — remarkably — Artaxerxes, whose decree had stopped the work of Ezra's day (4:21) and who would later authorize Ezra's own mission (7:12–26). The author is including all three Persians because the building was the result of a divine purpose that ran through the reigns of multiple human kings, their agreements and their contradictions ultimately serving a single end. God's decree is the one that governs all the others.

Second, the date: 516 BC. Nebuchadnezzar burned the first temple in 586 BC. The second temple is completed in 516 BC. The difference is exactly seventy years — the precise period Jeremiah had prophesied (Jer. 25:11–12; 29:10). The precision is stunning. God's word is not approximate. He does not say "about seventy years" and mean sixty-eight or seventy-three. The second temple rises on the seventy-year mark as a public demonstration that the God of Israel keeps his word to the year. Begg: "The date of the completion is itself a sermon. God said seventy years; it was seventy years. That is the kind of God you are dealing with."

Third, the construction method: they built "through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah." The building was accomplished by human hands, royal funding, and managerial leadership — but the author attributes it to prophetic preaching. The word of God was the engine. Everything else was the machinery the word drove. This is the New Testament's understanding of church growth as well: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth" (1 Cor. 3:6) — and the planting was done through the preaching of the word.

sections.title: Dedication and Passover: The Second Exodus Complete (vv. 16–22)
sections.commentary:
The dedication of the temple (vv. 16–17) is deliberately modest compared to Solomon's. There is no Shekinah glory descending, no fire from heaven, no ark of the covenant (it had been lost in 586 BC and was never recovered). The offerings are substantial — 100 bulls, 200 rams, 400 lambs, 12 male goats as a sin offering for all Israel — but far fewer than the 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep of Solomon's dedication (1 Kgs. 8:63). The twelve male goats (v. 17) are the most theologically pointed detail: one goat per tribe, for all Israel, even though the returnees are predominantly Judah and Benjamin. The remnant that has returned represents and intercedes for the whole. This is the priestly-representative logic of the entire restoration project.

The Passover (vv. 19–22) is the liturgical capstone. The community gathers to celebrate the feast of deliverance — the memorial of the first Exodus — in the newly completed temple of the second return. The timing (the fourteenth day of the first month, Nisan) is precise Mosaic legislation (Exod. 12:6; Lev. 23:5). The note that "the Levites had purified themselves together, all of them were clean" (v. 20) — unusual because normally priests purified themselves — reflects the unusual circumstance of the restoration community: it is the Levites who slaughter the Passover lamb for all Israel in an act of extraordinary priestly generosity.

Most striking of all is verse 21: "It was eaten by the people of Israel who had returned from exile, and also by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD, the God of Israel." The Passover community includes not just ethnic returnees but proselytes who had separated themselves from pagan practices. This is the missional note that runs through the entire restoration narrative: the covenant community is defined not by ethnicity but by covenant allegiance. Those who worship the LORD, the God of Israel, are welcome at the table. The same logic governs the new covenant community gathered at the Lord's table (Gal. 3:28).

The first half of Ezra closes on a note of joy: "the LORD had made them joyful and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria to them, so that he aided them in the work of the house of God, the God of Israel" (v. 22). The king of "Assyria" is Darius the Persian — the title is deliberately archaic, reminding the reader that the great empires are interchangeable instruments in God's hands. More important, the joy is God-given: the LORD made them joyful. The same God who stirred their spirits to return (1:5) now makes them joyful in completion. From the first stirring to the final joy, the hand of God has been on this work.

6.theology:
The Faithfulness of God's Word. Ezra 6 is a public demonstration of the reliability of divine prophecy. Jeremiah said seventy years; it was seventy years. Isaiah named Cyrus; Cyrus appeared. The temple was promised; the temple stands. For the preacher, this is not merely a historical curiosity; it is the foundation of biblical hermeneutics. The God who kept his word to the year in 516 BC is the God who keeps every promise in Scripture. The certainty of future grace is grounded in the perfect record of past faithfulness.

The Second Exodus and Its Greater Fulfillment. The Passover celebration in vv. 19–22 closes the second Exodus typology. Israel returned from Babylon as from Egypt; the temple was rebuilt as the tabernacle was built; and now the Passover is celebrated in the new sanctuary. But this second Exodus is itself a type of the greater Exodus accomplished by Christ. Luke 9:31 describes the transfiguration conversation about his "departure" (exodos) — the cross and resurrection by which he leads his people out of the Egypt of sin. The Lord's Supper is the Passover of the new exodus, celebrated not in a rebuilt temple but "until he comes" (1 Cor. 11:26). Ezra 6 points both backward (to Egypt) and forward (to Calvary).
6.examples:
Then: The community that had wept at the foundation (3:12) now celebrates with joy at the completion (6:22). Twenty years of effort — foundation laid in 536 BC, building stopped, resumed, and finally finished in 516 BC — has culminated in a temple and a Passover. The joy is the joy of completed obedience, of the task finally accomplished. It is not the absence of grief (the temple was still less than Solomon's) but the presence of gratitude for what God had done through them in spite of everything against them.

Now: Every completed act of kingdom building — a church planted, a ministry established, a life transformed by the gospel — is an occasion for exactly this kind of joy. Not triumphalism (the building is still less than it should be; the new Jerusalem has not yet descended) but genuine, grateful celebration of what the hand of God has accomplished through the hands of his people. And every such celebration should include the Passover table — the Lord's Supper — as the reminder that all our building is predicated on the sacrifice that alone makes our approach to God possible.

7.title: The Scribe-Priest Arrives: Ezra, the Law, and the Hand of God
7.text: "For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel." (Ezra 7:10)
7.overview:
After the long narrative of chapters 1–6 (538–516 BC), chapter 7 opens with a jarring transition: "Now after this …" — and we are in 458 BC, fifty-eight years later. The temple is built and operating. But the community is in spiritual disorder: the people lack teachers, the law is unknown, and the community is drifting toward assimilation. Into this situation, God sends Ezra. His arrival is the turning point of the entire book, and the governing phrase of everything that follows is introduced in verse 6: "the hand of the LORD his God was on him."

Ezra is simultaneously a priest (direct descent from Aaron through Phinehas and Zadok, vv. 1–5) and a scribe — "a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses," v. 6. This dual identity is his defining characteristic. He is not an administrator but a theologian; not a politician but a teacher. And his method of work, stated in the programmatic verse 10, is the threefold pattern of all genuine ministry: study, do, teach. Personal formation precedes personal obedience; personal obedience precedes public ministry. The preacher who skips the first two steps will have nothing genuine to offer in the third.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Ezra's Genealogy, Qualification, and Program
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezra is introduced with an elaborate genealogy that connects him directly to Aaron and the Zadokite priestly line, establishing his credentials. His dual role as priest-scribe and his threefold ministry method (study, do, teach) are the theological foundations of everything that follows.
verseByVerse.theology: The conjunction of priestly identity and scribal expertise in Ezra is unique in the Old Testament and anticipates the New Testament vision of the pastor-teacher who is both a man of the text and a man of the altar. Ezra's genealogy is not status-display; it is theological argument — the one who will teach the law must be rooted in the covenant traditions he expounds.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The community in Jerusalem had been without systematic Torah-instruction for decades. The priests functioned at the altar; the Levites supervised the temple. But the kind of textual, expositional teaching that Ezra would bring was apparently absent. Now: The church that has liturgy without exposition, or sacrament without preached word, has the altar without Ezra. Both are needed; the Reformation insisted on recovering the preaching office alongside the liturgical one.

verseByVerse.quote: This is Ezra. He went up from Babylonia. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses that the LORD, the God of Israel, had given … (Ezra 7:6)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The genealogy of vv. 1–5 is not the full priestly record (it skips several generations compared to 1 Chr. 6:3–14) but highlights the key ancestors: Aaron, Eleazar, Phinehas (the zeal-for-God priest of Num. 25), Zadok (David's faithful high priest), and Seraiah (the last pre-exilic high priest, executed by Nebuchadnezzar in 2 Kgs. 25:18–21). The chain is deliberately selected to establish Ezra's credentials at every critical moment of Israel's priestly history. He is not a newcomer to the tradition; he is the inheritor of the fullest and most tested priestly lineage.

But the genealogy immediately gives way to the professional description: "He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses." The Hebrew is sofer mahir be-torat moshe — a skilled, expert, rapid writer in the Torah. The word mahir (skilled, expert) suggests mastery: Ezra does not merely know the law; he has internalized it to the point of fluency. Derek Kidner compares him to a great musician who no longer thinks about technique — the law has become second nature. This is what Paul means by "the word of Christ dwelling in you richly" (Col. 3:16): not casual acquaintance but resident expertise.

"The hand of the LORD his God was on him" (v. 6b) — introduced here for the first time — is the theological key to the second half of the book. The phrase occurs seven times in chapters 7–8 (7:6, 9, 28; 8:18, 22, 31), creating a theological drumbeat: every significant event, every supply granted, every journey completed, every provision given is attributed to the hand of God. Iain Duguid: "The repetition is not stylistic padding; it is theological insistence. The author will not let the reader credit human competence or Persian generosity for what God has accomplished."

verseByVerse.quote: For on the first day of the first month he began to go up from Babylonia, and on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem, for the good hand of his God was on him. (Ezra 7:9)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The journey from Babylon to Jerusalem is approximately 900 miles and took four months — from the first of Nisan to the first of Ab (roughly April to August). The route followed the Fertile Crescent northward and then southwest, avoiding the Arabian Desert. Ezra traveled with a significant company (the list in chapter 8 totals approximately 1,500 men plus women and children) carrying considerable wealth (8:26–27). No military escort was requested (8:22). The journey was completed in four months under the hand of God.

The dating formula is precise and liturgically freighted: the first day of the first month is the day the tabernacle was first erected (Exod. 40:2). Ezra's departure from Babylon on that date may be coincidental — or the author may intend the echo deliberately, presenting Ezra's mission as a new "setting up of the sanctuary," this time not a physical structure but the law of God in the community's life. Williamson notes the literary care with which the dates are recorded throughout chapters 7–10, creating a chronological framework that invites the reader to see these events as divinely ordered.

The "good hand of his God" (v. 9) is distinguished by the adjective tov — good. This is not merely God's powerful hand but his beneficent hand, the hand that gives gifts to those he loves. The journey was providentially protected and prospered. No bandits attacked; no government stopped them; the provisions held; the party arrived intact. All of this is credited not to Ezra's planning or Persian infrastructure but to the goodness of God's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel. (Ezra 7:10)
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the programmatic verse of the second half of Ezra — arguably the most important verse in the book for understanding its theology of ministry. Three verbs, arranged in sequence: lidrosh (to study, to seek), la'asot (to do), ulelamad (to teach). Study precedes doing; doing precedes teaching. This is not merely Ezra's personal method; it is the divinely ordered logic of all biblical ministry.

The prior clause is equally important: "Ezra had set his heart." The verb is kun in the Hiphil — to establish, to prepare, to make firm. Ezra's commitment to study was not a mood or a season; it was a settled disposition of the will. He had made the study of Torah the fixed orientation of his interior life. This is what the Puritans called "the mortification of the affections" applied positively: the disciplined alignment of desire with God's word over years of patient reading and meditation.

The sequence study-do-teach has profound implications for preaching. A teacher who teaches what he has not studied has nothing to say; a teacher who studies but does not live what he studies has no authority to say it; a teacher who both knows and lives the text but never teaches it is hoarding what was given for others. Ezra holds all three together. MacArthur: "You cannot give what you do not have. You cannot call people to live what you are not living. And you must not keep to yourself what God has given you for the body." This is why the ministry of the word requires the total person — intellect, will, and affections — all submitted to the law of God.

Christologically: the one who perfectly embodied this threefold pattern was Jesus Christ, who not only studied the Scriptures (Luke 2:46–47; 4:16–21) but perfectly obeyed them ("I always do what pleases him," John 8:29) and taught them with an authority that astonished the crowds (Matt. 7:29). Ezra's threefold method is a type of the ministry of the one who came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5:17–19). The scribe-priest of the second temple points to the great High Priest who is also the Word made flesh.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–26 — Artaxerxes' Letter: Imperial Support for Torah Ministry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter of Artaxerxes I (vv. 12–26) is one of the most remarkable documents in the Old Testament: a pagan emperor commissioning a Jewish scribe-priest to teach the law of Moses throughout the province of Judah, with unlimited financial support and full legal authority. The letter may be the most thoroughly argued case for state-supported religious education in the ancient world.
verseByVerse.theology: The letter demonstrates that God can use imperial power to advance Torah-education, just as he used it to fund temple-building in chapters 1–6. The commission Artaxerxes gives Ezra — to appoint judges who know the law and to teach those who do not — is essentially a program of national biblical literacy underwritten by the Persian treasury. Providence underwrites the ministry of the word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Persian administrative system, with its provincial governors and regional courts, became the vehicle for establishing Torah as the legal framework of the Judean community. The imperial letter gave Ezra's teaching authority the force of law. Now: The preacher's authority is not imperial but apostolic — grounded in the word of God itself, not in civil structures. But the principle holds: those who preach the word should preach with full confidence in its authority, knowing that the King of kings has commissioned them.

verseByVerse.quote: Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven. Peace. And now I decree … (Ezra 7:12–13)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter of Artaxerxes is presented in its original Aramaic (v. 12 through 26 is in Aramaic, the imperial lingua franca, unlike the surrounding Hebrew narrative). Its authenticity is widely accepted by conservative scholars and viewed as plausible even by many critical scholars, given its close correspondence to the conventions of Persian imperial correspondence. The address — "Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven" — is in standard Persian chancellery form, and the title "God of heaven" (Aramaic Elah shemayya) is the standard Persian-era designation for the God of Israel.

Verse 13 grants permission to any Israelite in the empire who wishes to go with Ezra to do so — a voluntary repatriation decree similar to Cyrus's original. Verses 14–19 grant Ezra extraordinary financial and administrative powers: he carries silver and gold from the king and his counselors (v. 15), is authorized to collect freewill offerings from throughout Babylon (v. 16), is given funds to purchase animals for sacrifice (v. 17), and is entrusted with the remaining silver for whatever "seems good to you and your brothers to do with the rest of the silver and gold" (v. 18). This is breathtaking administrative latitude given to a religious functionary: the Persian imperial treasury is being opened for the service of the God of Israel.

The theological point is made quietly by the narrative context: the same empire whose predecessor destroyed the temple is now funding its ministry. God's purposes are not thwarted by historical catastrophe; they are worked out through it and beyond it. Sproul was fond of pointing out that God does not merely "permit" such reversals — he ordains them.
